title: The Real Cost of Car Ownership in Canada (2026)
description: Complete breakdown of car ownership costs in Canada for 2026. Purchase payments, insurance by province, fuel vs EV, maintenance, parking, depreciation, and total annual cost.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: The average new car costs $12,000-$16,000 per year to own — not $849/month like your payment suggests. We break down every cost: payments, insurance by province, fuel vs EV, maintenance, and the silent killer — depreciation.

title: Parents Helping Kids Buy a First Home — FHSA, Gifting, Co-signing
description: How parents can help their kids buy a first home in Canada. FHSA strategies, gifted down payment rules, co-signing risks, Home Buyers' Plan from RRSP, and tax implications.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: With the average Canadian home price at $680K, many first-time buyers need help from parents. FHSA + HBP + gifted down payment can combine for a 20% down payment with maximum tax efficiency.

title: How Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Really Affects Your Finances
description: How Afterpay, Klarna, Affirm, and PayBright work in Canada. Hidden costs, behavioural traps, credit score impact, and when BNPL makes sense vs when it doesn't.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: BNPL users spend 20-40% more than they would paying upfront. Credit bureaus are now tracking usage. Here's what Afterpay, Klarna, and Affirm really cost you — and when they actually make sense.

title: RRIF vs Annuity: Which Is Better for Canadian Retirement Income?
description: Compare RRIF and annuity options for Canadian retirement income. RRIF minimum withdrawal rules, annuity pros and cons, hybrid strategies, and tax implications.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: RRIF gives you flexibility and control; an annuity gives you guaranteed income for life. Most retirees should use both. Here's how to build the optimal hybrid strategy for Canadian retirement income.

title: Building Credit as a Newcomer to Canada
description: Step-by-step guide to building credit as a newcomer to Canada. Secured cards, how credit scores work, timeline to good credit, and common mistakes immigrants make.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Your credit score from your home country doesn't transfer to Canada. Here's how to build good credit from zero in 6-12 months using secured cards, newcomer programs, and smart strategies.

title: Mortgage Renewal Strategies in a Changing Rate Environment
description: Smart mortgage renewal strategies for Canadians in 2026. When to start shopping, fixed vs variable analysis, negotiation tactics, and penalty math for breaking early.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Your lender's renewal letter is almost never their best offer. Start shopping 120 days before renewal, lock in rate holds, and negotiate with competing quotes. Here's the complete playbook for mortgage renewal in 2026.

title: Canada's 2026 Federal Budget: Every Tax Change That Affects Your Wallet
description: What to expect from Canada's 2026 Federal Budget: TFSA/RRSP limit increases, CCB changes, capital gains updates, housing affordability measures, climate incentives, small business tax changes, and income tier impact analysis.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Canada's 2026 Federal Budget preview: TFSA/RRSP limits, CCB adjustments, capital gains changes, housing affordability measures, climate incentives, and small business tax updates. Complete analysis of how every income tier is affected, plus action steps for your money.

title: How to Build a Simple Index ETF Portfolio in Canada (2026 Edition)
description: Step-by-step guide to building a low-cost, diversified index ETF portfolio in Canada. Asset allocation strategies, recommended ETFs (XEQT, VEQT, VGRO, VBAL), rebalancing rules, and tax-efficient investing in TFSA, RRSP, and taxable accounts.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Building a diversified portfolio doesn't require stock-picking or active management. A simple index ETF strategy—using one or two low-cost funds—can outperform most investors while requiring minimal maintenance. Here's exactly how to set it up in Canada.

title: TFSA vs RRSP vs FHSA: Where to Put Your Next Dollar in 2026
description: Which Canadian registered account deserves your next contribution dollar in 2026? Decision flowchart comparing TFSA, RRSP, and FHSA based on income, age, homeownership, and retirement timeline with worked examples.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: You have $10,000 to invest. Should it go to your TFSA, RRSP, or FHSA? The answer depends on your income, age, homeownership goals, and timeline. This guide provides a clear decision framework with real scenarios at every income level.

title: RESP Strategies: Maximize the CESG Before Your Kids Turn 18
description: How to maximize the Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) with optimal RESP contribution strategies, catch-up rules, provider comparisons, and what happens if your child doesn't go to school.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: The CESG gives you free money — up to $7,200 per child — but only if you contribute strategically. We break down optimal contribution schedules, catch-up rules, provider types, and what happens if your child skips post-secondary.

title: Lease vs Buy a Car in Canada: The Real Math
description: Total cost comparison of leasing vs buying a car in Canada. Hidden costs, tax implications for personal and business use, EV incentives, and a decision framework.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Leasing feels cheaper monthly but is it really? We run the full 6-year cost comparison on a $45K vehicle — lease vs finance vs cash — including hidden fees, tax write-offs, EV rebates, and depreciation curves.

title: Net Worth by Age in Canada: Where Do You Stand?
description: Canadian net worth benchmarks by age group using 2023 Statistics Canada data. Median vs average, regional differences, homeowner vs renter gap, and strategies to grow at every life stage.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: The median Canadian family has a net worth of $519,700 — but that number varies wildly by age, region, and homeownership. See where you stand with 2023 Stats Canada data and get strategies for every life stage.

title: GIC Rates in Canada 2026: Are They Still Worth It (and When to Lock In)
description: GIC rates in Canada are falling as the Bank of Canada cuts rates. Are GICs still worth it in 2026? Cashable vs non-redeemable, GIC laddering strategy, when GICs beat bonds and HISAs, and tax treatment.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: GIC rates in Canada are heading down after the Bank of Canada's aggressive rate-cutting cycle. With rates now in the 3.25%–4.25% range, are GICs still worth it? We break down cashable vs non-redeemable, the GIC laddering strategy, when GICs beat HISAs and bonds, and optimal tax treatment in registered vs non-registered accounts.

title: CPP at 60, 65, or 70? How to Decide When to Start Collecting
description: Should you take CPP at 60, 65, or 70? Breakeven analysis, 2026 payment amounts, impact of working while collecting, pension sharing, OAS/GIS interaction, and health considerations.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: The Canada Pension Plan start-age decision is one of the most consequential financial choices a Canadian retiree will make. The max CPP at 65 in 2026 is $1,364.60/month — take it at 60 and you get 36% less; wait until 70 and you get 42% more. We run the breakeven analysis, cover working while collecting, pension sharing, OAS/GIS interaction, and build a decision framework.

title: RRSP Deadline 2026: Last-Minute Strategies Before March 3rd
description: The RRSP contribution deadline for the 2025 tax year is March 3, 2026. Last-minute strategies including RRSP loans, spousal contributions, carry-forward deductions, and how to coordinate with TFSA and FHSA.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: The RRSP contribution deadline for the 2025 tax year is March 3, 2026. Whether you have $500 or $50,000 in contribution room, last-minute strategies like RRSP loans, spousal contributions, and carry-forward deductions can save you thousands. Here's your two-week game plan.

title: Canada's New Mortgage Rules: What the 2025-2026 Changes Mean for Buyers
description: Canada's biggest mortgage rule changes in a decade took effect in late 2024, expanding 30-year amortizations for first-time buyers, raising the insured mortgage cap to $1.5M, and opening secondary suite refinancing. Here's what every Canadian buyer and homeowner needs to know heading into spring 2026.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Canada's biggest mortgage rule changes in a decade took effect in late 2024, expanding 30-year amortizations for first-time buyers, raising the insured mortgage cap to $1.5M, and opening secondary suite refinancing. Here's what every Canadian buyer and homeowner needs to know heading into spring 2026.

title: Mortgage Renewal in 2026: What Every Canadian Needs to Know
description: Complete guide to renewing your mortgage in Canada in 2026. Payment shock calculations, fixed vs variable rates, switching lenders, penalty math, and strategies to prepare.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Roughly 1.2 million Canadian mortgages are up for renewal in 2026, and most borrowers face rates 2-3 percentage points higher than what they're paying. A $500K mortgage going from 1.89% to 4.5% means ~$700/month more. Here's how to prepare, negotiate, and minimize the impact.

title: What Canadians Get Wrong About Capital Gains Tax (2026 Update)
description: Comprehensive guide to Canadian capital gains tax in 2026. The new inclusion rate, principal residence exemption, LCGE, worked examples, and strategies to minimize your tax bill.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: The 2024 capital gains inclusion rate change confused a lot of Canadians. Here's what actually changed: individuals pay 50% inclusion on the first $250K of gains per year and 66.67% above that. We bust the myths, run worked examples, and show you how to legally minimize what you owe.

title: The True Cost of Raising a Child in Canada (2026 Edition)
description: Complete breakdown of raising a child in Canada from birth to 18. Includes provincial costs, CCB benefits, RESP strategies, and real cost estimates by age bracket.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Raising a child from birth to age 18 in Canada costs approximately $293,000 to $350,000, depending on your province and lifestyle choices. However, with the Canada Child Benefit (CCB) providing up to $180,000 over 18 years and smart RESP contributions capturing $7,200 in free government money, the net cost ranges from $113,000 to $170,000.

title: How Much Do You Really Need to Retire in Canada? The 2026 Numbers
description: Comprehensive guide to retirement savings in Canada for 2026. Learn about CPP, OAS, GIS, provincial cost differences, and how much you need for modest, comfortable, or affluent retirement.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Most Canadians will need between $400,000 and $1.2 million in retirement savings (excluding their home) to maintain their lifestyle, depending on their province and spending level. When combined with CPP and OAS, this translates to a retirement income ranging from $35,000 to $80,000+ annually.

title: FHSA vs RRSP for Your First Home: Which Should You Max Out First?
description: Comparing FHSA ($8K/year, $40K lifetime) vs RRSP HBP ($60K withdrawal) for first-time home buyers. Worked examples at $50K, $80K, $120K income with decision flowchart and optimal strategies.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Choosing between maxing your FHSA or RRSP for your first home down payment can save you thousands. We compare contribution limits ($8K vs $40K lifetime), tax treatment, repayment rules, and show worked examples at three income levels to help you decide which account to prioritize.

title: RRSP vs TFSA in 2026: Which Should Canadians Max Out First?
description: Discover whether to prioritize RRSP or TFSA contributions in 2026. Compare contribution limits, tax benefits, and income-based strategies to maximize your Canadian retirement savings.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Choosing between maximizing your RRSP or TFSA is one of the most common financial dilemmas facing Canadians. Both are powerful savings vehicles, but they work very differently—and the right choice depends heavily on your current income, future plans, and financial goals.

title: 2026 Canadian Tax Brackets Explained: Federal + Every Province
description: Complete 2026 Canadian tax brackets guide covering federal rates plus all 10 provinces and 3 territories. Includes CPP2 changes, basic personal amounts, and tax planning strategies.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Understanding Canadian tax brackets is essential for effective tax planning. In 2026, federal and provincial tax rates continue to evolve, with CPP2 enhancements and indexed basic personal amounts affecting your take-home pay.

title: First-Time Home Buyer's Guide to Canada in 2026
description: Complete 2026 guide for Canadian first-time home buyers. Learn about FHSA, HBP, down payment strategies, CMHC insurance, stress test rules, and provincial rebates to buy your first home.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Buying your first home in Canada can feel overwhelming, but 2026 brings several helpful programs including the First Home Savings Account (FHSA), enhanced Home Buyers' Plan, and provincial incentives that can make homeownership more accessible.

title: Avalanche vs Snowball: The Best Debt Payoff Strategy for Canadians
description: Avalanche vs Snowball debt payoff methods explained for Canadians. Learn which strategy works best for student loans, credit cards, and LOCs in 2026's interest rate environment.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: When you're carrying multiple debts—credit cards, student loans, car payments, lines of credit—choosing the right payoff strategy can save you thousands in interest and help you become debt-free faster. The two most popular approaches are the Avalanche and Snowball methods.

title: How to Value a Small Business in Canada: A Practical Guide
description: Learn how to value a small business in Canada using DCF, comparable multiples, and asset-based methods. Includes industry rules of thumb, goodwill calculations, and CRA tax implications.
author: Rick Minji
excerpt: Whether you're buying, selling, or seeking funding for a small business in Canada, understanding valuation is critical. Business valuation combines art and science—blending financial analysis with industry knowledge and market conditions.
